---
title: "Beyond LTE: electrons, H₂ and the Lyman–Werner bands"
---

The steady model and the TITAN runs assume LTE. @sec-lte showed that radiative rates control hydrogen's $n=2$
level at the photosphere. This chapter records two further questions about the same assumption, and the plan for
a non-LTE calculation.

## Could non-Saha electrons make H₂? {#sec-h2}

In the primordial gas, H$_2$ forms through the H$^-$ channel [@galli1998]:

$$
{\rm H} + e^- \to {\rm H}^- + \gamma \ (k_7),\qquad
{\rm H}^- + {\rm H} \to {\rm H_2} + e^- \ (k_8),\qquad
{\rm H}^- + \gamma \to {\rm H} + e^- \ (k_{\rm pd}).
$$ {#eq-hminus}

If free electrons were out of Saha equilibrium, for example left over from recombining shocked infall, more H$^-$
and hence more H$_2$ could form. We bound this with steady-state H$^-$, a photodetachment rate $k_{\rm pd}$ in a
diluted blackbody $W\,B_\nu(T_{\rm rad})$ with the cross section of @john1988, and no H$_2$ destruction, so the result
is an upper bound **[estimate]**.

At the extended-branch photosphere ($n_{\rm H} \approx 2\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-3}$, $T \approx 7300$ K, $W = 1/2$),
photodetachment beats associative detachment by $k_{\rm pd}/(k_8 n_{\rm H}) \approx 110$. The formation time
$n_{\rm H}/(k_8 n_{\rm H} n_{\rm H^-})$ is $10^4$ s in LTE and $4\times10^3$ to $2\times10^6$ s for electron fractions
between 0.5 and $10^{-3}$. In every case the equilibrium H$_2$ fraction at 7300 K, about $10^{-8}$, caps the result.
Catalysts change how fast the gas gets there, not where it ends up.

In the infall ($\dot M = 1\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, Lucy temperature) we integrate formation along the fall from $r$ to
$R$. Even with an electron fraction of 0.5 maintained throughout, the accumulated H$_2$ fraction stays below
$6\times10^{-7}$ for starting radii between $2R$ and $100R$. For $x_e = 10^{-3}$ it stays below $5\times10^{-9}$. The
reason is the same: photodetachment by the star's radiation is $10^4$–$10^6$ times faster than associative
detachment everywhere in the infall **[estimate]**.

## Can that small H₂ fraction matter for the Lyman–Werner bands? {#sec-lw}

Small abundances can still matter through line opacity, because the Lyman–Werner lines (11.2–13.6 eV) are strong.
The infall column outside $R$ is $N_{\rm H} = \int_R^\infty n_{\rm H}\,dr = 2\,n_{\rm H}(R)\,R \approx 3\times10^{24}$ cm$^{-2}$
at $\dot M = 1$. With the bounds above,

$$
N_{\rm H_2} \lesssim x_{\rm H_2} N_{\rm H} \approx 10^{16}\text{–}2\times10^{18}\ {\rm cm^{-2}} ,
$$ {#eq-nh2}

for electron fractions between $10^{-3}$ and 0.5 **[estimate]**. Individual Lyman–Werner lines become optically
thick, and self-shielding sets in, at $N_{\rm H_2} \sim 10^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$ [@draine1996]. So if H$_2$ is anywhere near
these bounds, the line cores of the Lyman–Werner bands are saturated across the infall. That would remove
photons in those lines from the escaping spectrum and shield the infall from H$_2$-dissociating radiation.

Two cautions keep this an open question rather than a result. First, the bounds ignore H$_2$ destruction by the
Lyman–Werner radiation of the star itself, which at $W \sim 10^{-2}$ of a 7000 K blackbody is strong; the actual
column could be far smaller. Second, line cores carry a small fraction of the flux unless the damping wings
overlap, which needs $N_{\rm H_2} \gtrsim 10^{20}$–$10^{21}$ cm$^{-2}$, above our bound. So the effect on the continuum
is expected to be small, while the effect on the line spectrum near 11–13.6 eV, and on photodissociation in the
infall, could be large **[interpretation]**. A self-consistent answer needs the H$_2$ chemistry with
self-shielding inside the non-LTE calculation below.

## The non-LTE plan {#sec-nlte-plan}

A time-independent non-LTE post-processing of steady and dynamical snapshots is justified because the
recombination times, about 10 s at the photosphere and at most a day in the infall, are much shorter than the
infall time $R/v_{\rm ff} \sim 2$ yr. The plan:

1. hydrogen with 10–15 levels plus continuum, then helium, on the steady extended- and compact-branch structures;
2. the Balmer break on both branches as the first observable;
3. H$_2$ and H$^-$ chemistry with Lyman–Werner self-shielding in the infall (@sec-lw);
4. the same post-processing on TITAN snapshots once the infall runs are stable (@sec-titan-qs).

This is the only part of the programme where GPUs are expected to pay off: the full non-LTE problem has many
frequencies and levels per zone, while the radiation hydrodynamics is 1D with seven unknowns per zone.
